# Testing at Boundaries + TDD loop

*LLM first draft · human-edited once · frozen*

## Tests belong at the boundary

You already know the Target Interface is the one part of an Exercise you
cannot change. This Module makes that constraint the whole point: tests belong
at that boundary and nowhere else. A test written against the Target Interface
says **what the code must do for its caller**. A test written against an
internal class says *how the code happens to do it today* — and it breaks the
moment you improve the design, which is exactly when you need it most.

A test earns its keep two ways: it fails when behavior is wrong, and it stays
green when behavior is preserved. Internals-coupled tests fail both duties.
They can pass while the observable behavior is broken — they check a helper,
not the outcome — and they fail during a refactor that changed nothing a
caller could notice. When that happens you either abandon the refactor or
rewrite the tests, and a rewritten test proves little: it was written to match
the new code, not to constrain it.

Boundary tests give you the opposite deal. Everything behind the Target
Interface is yours — rename it, split it, merge it, delete it. If the Test
Suite stays green, the behavior survived. This is what makes the Test Suite in
every Exercise the trustworthy artifact: it does not care how you got there.

Two countable signs your tests sit at the wrong depth:

- Read the `using` directives and constructor calls in the test file. Count
  the types a real caller of the Target Interface would never touch. Every one
  is a test reaching into internals.
- Rename a private method or an internal class — behavior unchanged. Count the
  tests that fail or stop compiling. Each one was coupled to structure, not
  behavior.

## Hidden dependencies surface at the boundary

Volatile dependencies the policy grabs for itself — the system clock, the file
system, the network — show up in tests as tolerance assertions, sleeps, and
flakes. `DateTime.UtcNow` read inside the policy means expiry "in 14 days"
can only be tested by re-doing the arithmetic and allowing a few seconds of
slack. The fix is Module 2's move seen from the testing side: the dependency
enters through the boundary as a small C# `interface` — a clock, a store —
and the Test Suite hands in a fake it fully controls. Then the exact boundary
moment — the last legal second, the first expired one — becomes a plain
assertion instead of a tolerance window.

## The TDD loop, and small steps as the speed limit

The loop is three moves, repeated:

1. **Red** — write one failing test against the Target Interface. Run it and
   read the failure: it must fail for the right reason (the behavior is
   missing), not a typo or a setup error.
2. **Green** — write the least code that makes it pass. Not the best code, not
   the general solution. The least.
3. **Refactor** — with the Test Suite green, improve everything behind the
   boundary. Tests do not change in this step. The urge to edit a test while
   refactoring means either the test was written against internals, or the
   behavior is changing under the refactor's name.

Small steps are not a style preference; they are the speed limit that keeps
the loop informative. One test per loop. After each Green, state in one
sentence what a caller can now rely on that they could not before — a sentence
that needs "and" was two steps. And keep each change small enough that when
the suite goes red, you know which edit did it without a debugger: **the
failure locates itself**. Bisecting your own last ten minutes of work means
the steps were too big.

## How this runs in your Exercises

- In a construct-type Exercise, run `dotnet test` before writing anything and
  count the failures — that number is your worklist. Make one test pass at a
  time, in the order that needs the least code, and build nothing that no red
  test currently demands.
- In a refactor-type Exercise, the Test Suite starts green and must stay green
  after every small step.
- Either way, finish with this check: could someone rebuild the implementation
  from the Target Interface and the Test Suite alone? If yes, your tests
  describe behavior.

This Module's Exercises plant exactly these Smells: a surface widened so tests
could watch the internals run, and a clock begging to be read instead of
injected. The Behavioral Checklist is how you catch them in your own code from
now on.

modelExamples.caption: The test stopped pinning the pipeline: every assertion now goes through the Target Interface, so the steps, fields, and audit log behind it can be renamed, merged, or deleted while the Test Suite stays green. Structure-coupled tests fail on refactors; boundary tests fail only on broken behavior.

The real clock made expiry untestable — the before side re-implements the arithmetic and allows five seconds of slack. With time injected at the boundary, the Test Suite drives a fake clock to the exact expiry instant and asserts behavior, not arithmetic.

The everything-test split into one rule per test. A failing name now states exactly which rule broke, no assert is hidden behind an earlier failure — and the list of names doubles as the TDD worklist: each was written red-first, made green with the least code, then refactored behind the boundary.

exercises.title: Shrink a basket pricer's test-widened surface
exercises.smell: Testing through the internals: the basket pricer was made "testable" by widening its surface. Public step methods the old tests drove in sequence, public fields exposing intermediate pipeline state, and a public discount audit log exist only so tests could watch the pipeline run — renaming one step broke tests while every price stayed identical. All the behavior is observable at the Target Interface; hide the steps and the state again, with the boundary Test Suite green the whole time.

exercises.title: Grow a rate limiter red-to-green behind a fake clock
exercises.smell: The construct temptation is to skip the loop and the boundary at once: implement everything in one sitting against the real clock — DateTime.UtcNow read inside the policy — leaving the sliding window testable only by actually waiting it out. Time is the volatile dependency: the limiter receives IClock through its constructor, the Test Suite drives a fake clock, and you work one red test at a time, top to bottom.

checklistQuestions.prompt: Grep your Test Suite for every type and member that is not on the Target Interface — concrete classes, public fields, step methods. Beyond the single construction line (the CreateX() factory), is the count zero?

options.label: Yes — the tests touch only the boundary
No — at least one test reaches into internals

checklistQuestions.prompt: Rename every private member and extract one helper class — behavior unchanged — then rerun the Test Suite. Did it stay green with zero edits to any test?

options.label: No — a test broke or needed editing

checklistQuestions.prompt: Comment out one business rule in the implementation and rerun the Test Suite (restore it after). Did at least one test fail, with a name that states the rule you broke?

options.label: Yes — the failure named the broken rule
No — all green, or the failure said nothing
